report.answer_text:
The October 20, 2025 AWS outage started with a software bug in the automated DNS system for DynamoDB, Amazon’s managed database, in its Northern Virginia (us-east-1) region. Two automated updates ran in an unexpected order—a *race condition*—leaving the database’s regional address with an empty DNS record. Applications that depended on that address could no longer connect. (aws.amazon.com)
The failure spread beyond the database. Even after AWS fixed DNS, customers had trouble launching new EC2 virtual servers, and faulty load-balancer health checks caused further connection failures. AWS Lambda and other cloud services were also affected. The main incident lasted about 14½ hours. (aws.amazon.com)
Users around the world felt the effects. Disrupted services included Snapchat, Signal, Slack, Canva, Roblox, Fortnite, and Amazon’s own Ring and Alexa. The failure began in one AWS region, but services used worldwide depended on it. (thousandeyes.com)

quotes.text: The incident was triggered by a latent defect within the service’s automated DNS management system that caused endpoint resolution failures for DynamoDB.

The root cause of this issue was a latent race condition in the DynamoDB DNS management system that resulted in an incorrect empty DNS record for the service’s regional endpoint (dynamodb.us-east-1.amazonaws.com) that the automation failed to repair.

pages.quote_reason: The quotes back the core claim that the incident was triggered by a latent software defect (race condition) in the automated DynamoDB DNS management system affecting the us-east-1 endpoint, but they do not state the October 20, 2025 date or the Northern Virginia location.
pages.page_reason: The page states the DynamoDB disruption was triggered by a latent defect in the service's automated DNS management system (a latent race condition) in the N. Virginia (us-east-1) Region, and that it began at 11:48 PM PDT on October 19, so the claim's 'October 20' start date and framing as the outage start is only partly aligned, though the page explicitly says the event began October 19 at 11:48 PM PDT.

quotes.text: The root cause of this issue was a latent race condition in the DynamoDB DNS management system that resulted in an incorrect empty DNS record for the service’s regional endpoint (dynamodb.us-east-1.amazonaws.com) that the automation failed to repair.
The timing of these events triggered the latent race condition.
At the same time that this clean-up process was invoked, the first Enactor (which had been unusually delayed) applied its much older plan to the regional DDB endpoint, overwriting the newer plan.
As this plan was deleted, all IP addresses for the regional endpoint were immediately removed.

pages.quote_reason: The quotes state a latent race condition in the DynamoDB DNS system that left the us-east-1 regional endpoint with an empty DNS record, and that a delayed first Enactor applied an older plan over a newer one, which matches the claimed out-of-order automated updates.
pages.page_reason: The page states that a latent race condition between two DNS Enactors let an older plan overwrite a newer one, after which clean-up deleted it and removed all IP addresses, leaving an incorrect empty DNS record for the regional DynamoDB endpoint.

quotes.text: When this issue occurred at 11:48 PM PDT, all systems needing to connect to the DynamoDB service in the N. Virginia (us-east-1) Region via the public endpoint immediately began experiencing DNS failures and failed to connect to DynamoDB.

The root cause of this issue was a latent race condition in the DynamoDB DNS management system that resulted in an incorrect empty DNS record for the service’s regional endpoint (dynamodb.us-east-1.amazonaws.com) that the automation failed to repair.
As this plan was deleted, all IP addresses for the regional endpoint were immediately removed.

pages.quote_reason: The quotes state that systems connecting to DynamoDB's regional public endpoint in us-east-1 immediately began experiencing DNS failures and failed to connect, because the regional endpoint's DNS record was empty and all its IP addresses were removed.
pages.page_reason: The page states that the DNS failure removed all IP addresses for the regional endpoint (dynamodb.us-east-1.amazonaws.com), and that systems connecting via the public endpoint failed to connect to DynamoDB, which supports the claim that dependent applications could not connect.

Between 11:48 PM PDT on October 19 and 1:50 PM PDT on October 20, customers experienced increased EC2 API error rates, latencies, and instance launch failures in the N. Virginia (us-east-1) Region.

quotes.text: This was caused by health check failures in the NLB fleet, which resulted in increased connection errors on some NLBs.
The alternating health check results increased the load on the health check subsystem, causing it to degrade, resulting in delays in health checks and triggering automatic AZ DNS failover to occur.
In this case, an application experienced increased connection errors if the remaining healthy capacity was insufficient to carry the application load.

pages.quote_reason: The quotes state that health check failures in the NLB fleet resulted in increased connection errors on some NLBs, which backs the claim's causal link between health checks and further connection failures.
pages.page_reason: The page states that NLB health check failures caused nodes and backend targets to be removed from DNS and led to increased connection errors for some load balancers, which directly supports the claim that faulty load-balancer health checks caused further connection failures.
